title: Prophecy and Its Failure as a Pattern
description: Early Christians, the Montanists and the year 1000 meet an end that does not arrive

concepts.title: The Kingdom That Was Coming Soon
concepts.contentHtml:
The earliest Christian texts expect the end soon. Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians, usually dated about 50 CE and probably the oldest surviving Christian writing, tells believers that "we who are alive, who are left" will be caught up to meet the Lord in the air. In Mark's Gospel Jesus says that "this generation will not pass away" before these things happen (Mark 13:30), and that some standing with him "will not taste death" before they see the kingdom come with power (Mark 9:1). The Greek word for Christ's expected arrival is parousia, "presence" or "arrival", the term used for the visit of a ruler.

The generation passed, and later texts show the strain. The Gospel of John ends by correcting a rumor that the beloved disciple would live until Jesus returned: Jesus, the text insists, never said that (John 21:23). The Second Letter of Peter, which most critical scholars date to the early second century and regard as written in Peter's name by a later author, answers "scoffers" who ask "Where is the promise of his coming?" With the Lord, it says, one day is as a thousand years, and the delay is patience that gives sinners time to repent.

Whether Jesus himself expected an imminent end is a long-running scholarly debate. Albert Schweitzer's Quest of the Historical Jesus (1906) portrayed him as an apocalyptic prophet whose expectation went unfulfilled, and E. P. Sanders, Dale Allison and Bart Ehrman defend versions of that view. Others, including John Dominic Crossan and Marcus Borg, argue that much of the apocalyptic material came from his followers.

concepts.title: Montanus and the New Jerusalem
concepts.contentHtml:
In the second half of the second century, in Phrygia in west-central Anatolia, a recent convert named Montanus began to prophesy in ecstatic states. Ancient writers disagree on the date. Eusebius puts the start around 172 CE, Epiphanius in the 150s, and modern scholars argue across that range. Two women, Priscilla (or Prisca) and Maximilla, became prophets of the movement and by some reports drew more followers than Montanus himself. Adherents called it the New Prophecy; opponents called it the Phrygian heresy, and later Montanism.

The New Prophecy demanded strict fasting, discouraged remarriage and flight from persecution, and announced that the heavenly Jerusalem would come down at Pepuza and Tymion, two small Phrygian towns. The fourth-century heresy-hunter Epiphanius quotes Maximilla as saying that after her there would be no more prophet, but the end. An anonymous opponent quoted by Eusebius mocked the movement because more than thirteen years after Maximilla's death neither the wars she had foretold nor the end had come.

Failure did not finish the movement. Tertullian of Carthage, a major Latin Christian writer of his day, defended the New Prophecy from about 207 CE. Montanist communities lasted for centuries. In the sixth century the emperor Justinian moved against them, and around 550 John of Ephesus led an expedition that destroyed their shrine at Pepuza, built over the tombs of the founders. Almost everything known about Montanism comes from hostile writers, so how its members understood their delayed New Jerusalem is mostly lost.

concepts.title: The Year 1000: Terror or Myth?
concepts.contentHtml:
A famous story holds that as the year 1000 approached, Europe froze in terror. Peasants abandoned their fields, nobles gave their estates to monasteries, and crowds waited in churches for the end. The full story took shape much later, in early modern chronicles and above all in nineteenth-century Romantic history such as Jules Michelet's History of France. Historians in the late nineteenth century went back to the sources and found little to support a general panic.

Several facts work against the legend. Counting years from the birth of Christ (anno Domini) was spreading but not universal, and many documents still dated by a ruler's regnal years. Regions began the year on different days, such as Christmas, 25 March or Easter. And charters that open with phrases like "as the end of the world approaches" use a stock formula found long before and after 1000.

Some sources do record expectation. Abbo of Fleury, writing in the late 990s, recalled hearing as a young man a preacher in Paris announce that Antichrist would come when a thousand years were complete, and he reported a rumor that the world would end in a year when the Annunciation (25 March) fell on Good Friday. The monk Rodulfus Glaber, writing in the 1030s and 1040s, linked portents and famine to the millennium of Christ's birth and of his Passion in 1033. In the 1990s Richard Landes argued that expectation around 1000 and 1033 was real and that clerical writers played it down afterward. Critics such as Sylvain Gouguenheim (1999) replied that the evidence shows ordinary piety, not mass fear. Many historians now settle between the two: no continent-wide panic, but real pockets of expectation.

title: Münster, 1534 to 1535
description: An Anabaptist New Jerusalem, a king, a siege and three iron cages

concepts.title: From Prophecy to Takeover
concepts.contentHtml:
Münster, the chief city of a prince-bishopric in Westphalia, became the setting for an Anabaptist takeover during the Radical Reformation. In the early 1530s its preacher Bernhard Rothmann led the city from Catholicism toward Lutheranism and then further, toward Anabaptist teaching that rejected infant baptism in favor of adult baptism. Meanwhile in the Netherlands, followers of the lay preacher Melchior Hoffman expected the end soon. Hoffman had predicted Christ's return for 1533 and was in prison in Strasbourg, where he died about ten years later.

Leadership of the Dutch movement passed to Jan Matthys, a baker from Haarlem who claimed to be the prophet Enoch and who replaced Hoffman's patient waiting with an armed, imminent kingdom. His envoys, among them a young tailor and former innkeeper from Leiden named Jan Beukelszoon (Jan of Leiden), reached Münster in January 1534 and began baptizing adults. Matthys arrived in February. On 23 February 1534 Anabaptists and their sympathizers won the council elections, and the cloth merchant Bernd Knipperdolling became mayor. Many Catholics and Lutherans had already left; those who remained and refused rebaptism were driven out, while Anabaptists from the Netherlands and Westphalia streamed in to the New Jerusalem.

The prince-bishop, Franz von Waldeck, began a siege almost at once, later backed by Catholic and Lutheran princes alike. Matthys announced that judgment would fall at Easter. On Easter Sunday, 5 April 1534, he rode out against the besiegers with a small band (accounts range from about a dozen to thirty men) and was killed; his head was displayed on a pole. The date had failed, but the city did not surrender. Jan of Leiden took over.

concepts.title: King Jan and the Besieged Kingdom
concepts.contentHtml:
Jan of Leiden, about 25 years old, governed by revelation. He replaced the council with twelve elders on the model of the tribes of Israel, imposed a strict moral code with death as the penalty for many offenses, and enforced community of goods: money was collected and private property largely abolished. Books other than the Bible were reportedly burned. In the summer of 1534 he introduced polygamy, citing the Old Testament patriarchs and a population in which women of marriageable age outnumbered men, by common estimates about three to one. Resistance flared. An armed revolt led by the blacksmith Heinrich Mollenhecke briefly took Jan and the preachers prisoner, and after it collapsed dozens of rebels were executed.

In September 1534, after the defenders beat off a major assault, a prophet named Johann Dusentschur proclaimed Jan king, the successor of David with a claim to rule the world. He held court in robes and crowns made from requisitioned gold, with Divara, the widow of Matthys, as chief queen among about sixteen wives. Sources report that in June 1535 he beheaded one wife, Elisabeth Wandscherer, in the market square after she asked to leave; some historians suspect the story was embellished later.

The siege tightened into a blockade, and by spring 1535 famine was severe. Much of what is known comes from two hostile insiders: Heinrich Gresbeck, a defender who escaped and helped the besiegers, and Hermann von Kerssenbrock, a Catholic who had been a schoolboy in the city and wrote his history decades later. Both had reasons to make the kingdom look as monstrous as possible, which historians weigh before repeating their accounts.

concepts.title: The Fall, the Cages and the Legacy
concepts.contentHtml:
On the night of 24 to 25 June 1535 two defectors, one of them Gresbeck, guided the bishop's soldiers through a gate. Fighting went on into the next day. Several hundred defenders were killed in the storming and the killings that followed, women and children were expelled, and Divara was among those executed. Rothmann disappeared in the fighting; his fate is unknown. Total deaths over the whole siege are usually put in the thousands, but the figures in the sources vary widely.

Jan of Leiden, Bernd Knipperdolling and Bernd Krechting were kept alive for months, interrogated and displayed. On 22 January 1536 they were publicly tortured with red-hot tongs and killed in front of St Lambert's Church on the Prinzipalmarkt. Their bodies were hung from the church tower in three iron cages as a warning. The remains were eventually removed but the cages stayed. When the tower was rebuilt they were taken down in 1881, and the originals were rehung on the new tower in 1898; they still hang there today. In 1987 the artist Lothar Baumgarten placed a dim light in each cage for the city's Skulptur Projekte exhibition.

For generations Catholic and Lutheran writers cited Münster as proof that rejecting infant baptism led to sedition. Menno Simons, a Dutch priest who broke with Rome in 1536, rebuilt the northern Anabaptist movement on strict nonviolence, and the Mennonites take their name from him. Historians read Münster in different ways. Norman Cohn's The Pursuit of the Millennium (1957) placed it in a long line of revolutionary millenarianism, Marxist writers saw an early communist rising, and recent historians stress local politics and the pressure of the siege.

title: Sabbatai Zevi, the Messiah of 1665
description: A prophet in Gaza, a wave across the Jewish world, and a messiah who converted to Islam

concepts.title: Sabbatai and Nathan
concepts.contentHtml:
Sabbatai Zevi was born in 1626 in Smyrna (modern Izmir), a booming Ottoman port. Tradition puts his birth on the Ninth of Av, the fast that mourns the destruction of the Temple and, in some traditions, the birthday of the messiah. He studied Kabbalah and swung, as friends and enemies both recorded, between periods of exaltation and deep depression; Gershom Scholem thought the pattern resembled what psychiatry calls manic depression. In exalted states he performed what followers called ma'asim zarim, "strange acts": pronouncing the forbidden name of God, celebrating festivals on the wrong days, and in Salonica staging a wedding with a Torah scroll. Rabbis expelled him from several cities, and he wandered through Constantinople, Cairo and Jerusalem. In Cairo he married Sarah, a refugee from the massacres of Jews in Poland and Ukraine in 1648 to 1649, who reputedly said she was destined to marry the messiah.

The decisive figure was a young scholar in Gaza, Abraham Nathan Ashkenazi, known as Nathan of Gaza (c. 1643 to 1680), who had a reputation as a visionary able to diagnose the state of a person's soul. In the spring of 1665 Sabbatai came to him seeking relief from his torments. After a vision around the festival of Shavuot, Nathan told him instead that he was the messiah, and at the end of May 1665, at Nathan's urging, Sabbatai declared himself the redeemer.

Nathan became the movement's theologian and publicist. His letters, copied and forwarded across the diaspora, called for penance and set out a timetable in which Sabbatai would soon take the crown from the Ottoman sultan without war. Many Jerusalem rabbis rejected the claim, and Nathan declared Gaza the new holy city.

concepts.title: The Wave and the Turban
concepts.contentHtml:
News moved along the trade routes of the Mediterranean and beyond. In autumn 1665 Sabbatai returned to Smyrna, and in December he took over its synagogue, deposed opponents and handed out the kingdoms of the world to followers. By early 1666 the excitement had reached Constantinople, Salonica, Venice, Livorno, Amsterdam, Hamburg, Poland, Morocco and Yemen. Communities undertook intense penitence through fasting and ritual immersion, and some people sold houses and goods to prepare for the journey to the Land of Israel. Glückel of Hameln, a Jewish businesswoman whose memoir is a major source for her world, recalled that her father-in-law sent casks of linen and dried food to her house in Hamburg, packed for the voyage, where they stood for more than a year. Not everyone believed; opponents existed in many communities, though in 1666 many kept quiet.

In early 1666 Sabbatai sailed for Constantinople and was arrested on the orders of the grand vizier. Rather than being executed he was held, after about two months, in the fortress of Abydos on the Dardanelles near Gallipoli, where visitors came in such numbers that the prison became a messianic court. In September 1666 Nehemiah ha-Kohen, a kabbalist from Poland, visited, disputed with him and then denounced him to the authorities. Sabbatai was brought before the court of Sultan Mehmed IV at Edirne and given a choice that later accounts describe as conversion or death. On 16 September 1666 (some sources say the 15th) he put on the turban, took the name Aziz Mehmed Efendi and accepted a salaried post at the palace as a gatekeeper.

concepts.title: After the Apostasy
concepts.contentHtml:
The conversion shattered the movement but did not end it. Many believers returned quietly to ordinary Jewish life, and some communities later tore pages from their record books to bury the episode. Nathan, however, gave the scandal a theology. In Lurianic Kabbalah, holy sparks are trapped in the kelippot, the "husks" of evil, and ordinary Jews free them by keeping the commandments. Nathan argued that the messiah's task was harder: he had to descend into the realm of the husks himself, which meant appearing to betray his faith. On this view the apostasy was itself part of the redemption.

Sabbatai lived ambiguously between Islam and Judaism until the authorities exiled him in 1673 to Dulcigno (Ulcinj, in modern Montenegro), where he died in 1676. Some followers imitated his conversion. The largest group conversion came in Salonica in 1683, and its members became the Dönmeh (Turkish for "converts"), outwardly Muslim, privately keeping Sabbatian rites in Hebrew and Ladino, and marrying only among themselves. The community split into three branches. After the Greek-Turkish population exchange of 1923 most members moved to Turkey, where they largely assimilated and became targets of conspiracy theories.

Modern understanding rests on Gershom Scholem's Sabbatai Sevi: The Mystical Messiah (Hebrew 1957, English 1973). Scholem argued that Lurianic Kabbalah had spread so widely that Jews everywhere were primed for redemption, and he rejected the older view that the 1648 to 1649 massacres were the main cause, noting the movement's strength in Sephardi lands far from Poland. Later scholars, notably Moshe Idel, doubt that Lurianic ideas were so widespread before 1665, and others emphasize Nathan's skill as a propagandist and the wider climate of expectation in the 1660s.

title: The Great Disappointment, 1844
description: William Miller's arithmetic, a date in October, and the churches built from the wreckage

concepts.title: William Miller's Arithmetic
concepts.contentHtml:
William Miller (1782 to 1849) was a farmer in Low Hampton, New York, a veteran of the War of 1812 and a former deist who returned to the Baptist faith around 1816. Determined to answer skeptics, he worked through the Bible with a concordance and became convinced that its prophecies formed a timetable. He built his count on Daniel 8:14: "Unto two thousand and three hundred days; then shall the sanctuary be cleansed."

Miller read each prophetic day as a year, a principle with a long Protestant pedigree. He began the count in 457 BCE, the year he assigned to the decree of the Persian king Artaxerxes sending Ezra to Jerusalem, and tied it to the "seventy weeks" of Daniel 9. Adding 2,300 years brought him to about 1843. The cleansing of the sanctuary, he decided, meant the purification of the earth by fire at Christ's return. He reached this conclusion around 1818 but began preaching publicly only in 1831.

Miller became a national figure through Joshua V. Himes, a Boston minister and publicist who from 1839 organized newspapers such as Signs of the Times and The Midnight Cry, camp meetings, a huge tent and printed prophetic charts. Believers came from many denominations. Miller himself estimated that 50,000 to 100,000 people accepted his views, and far more heard them. Pressed for precision, he said Christ would come sometime between 21 March 1843 and 21 March 1844, a Jewish year by his reckoning. That year passed, and so did a revised date in April 1844. Himes admitted in print that they had been mistaken about the precise time, but the movement held together, waiting.

concepts.title: 22 October 1844
concepts.contentHtml:
In August 1844, at a camp meeting in Exeter, New Hampshire, a Millerite preacher named Samuel S. Snow presented what became known as the "seventh-month message". He argued that Christ fulfilled the Jewish festivals on their own calendar: his death had matched Passover in the spring, so his return would match the Day of Atonement, the tenth day of the seventh month. By the Karaite Jewish reckoning Snow used, that fell on 22 October 1844. The idea swept the movement. Miller, hesitant at first, accepted it in early October.

In the final weeks many believers left crops unharvested, closed shops, settled debts and gave money away. Then the day, a Tuesday, passed. Hiram Edson, a farmer near Port Gibson, New York, later wrote: "Our fondest hopes and expectations were blasted, and such a spirit of weeping came over us as I never experienced before... We wept, and wept, till the day dawn." Another believer, Henry Emmons, recalled that he waited all Tuesday and "dear Jesus did not come". The event became known as the Great Disappointment.

One popular image needs correcting. Newspapers of the time and later reminiscences describe Millerites in white "ascension robes" waiting on rooftops and hilltops. Investigations, first by the Adventist writer Francis D. Nichol in the 1940s and since by other historians, found almost no reliable contemporary evidence for the robes; the story lived mainly in mockery. The hostility was real, though. Around this time Millerite meetings were disrupted, property was vandalized, and in Ithaca, New York, a Millerite meeting house was burned.

concepts.title: Rebuilding from Disappointment
concepts.contentHtml:
The movement broke apart along the lines of how members explained the failure. Many returned to their old churches or left religion altogether. Miller and Himes concluded that the calculation had gone wrong somewhere, refused new dates and kept expecting the advent soon; a conference at Albany, New York, in 1845 set out this moderate position, and from that wing came the Advent Christian Church, organized in 1860. Some "spiritualizers" decided that Christ had come invisibly, into believers' hearts, and a number of former Millerites joined the Shakers. Others set fresh dates in 1845 and after. Miller died in 1849, still expecting the end.

A small group read the failure differently: the date was right, but the event had been misidentified. In a later account, Hiram Edson said that on the morning of 23 October, crossing a field, he became convinced that the sanctuary of Daniel 8:14 was in heaven, and that on 22 October Christ had entered its inner room, the Most Holy Place, to begin a final phase of his work before returning. Developed by O. R. L. Crosier and others, this became the doctrine later called the investigative judgment.

Joined to the seventh-day Sabbath, taken from the Seventh Day Baptists and championed by the retired sea captain Joseph Bates, and to the visions of a young woman from Portland, Maine, Ellen Harmon (later Ellen G. White), whose first vision came in December 1844, these ideas grew into the Seventh-day Adventist Church, formally organized in 1863. It now reports more than 20 million baptized members worldwide.

title: When Prophecy Fails
description: A flying-saucer group in 1954, the famous study of it, its critics, and the Watch Tower's dates

concepts.title: Dorothy Martin and the Seekers
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1954 Dorothy Martin, a woman in her fifties living in Oak Park, a suburb of Chicago, began receiving messages through automatic writing. She had moved through Theosophical and other esoteric circles and had been involved with Dianetics. The messages came, she said, from beings on a planet called Clarion, above all from Sananda, whom she understood to be the present identity of Jesus. They warned that a great flood would destroy much of North America before dawn on 21 December 1954, and that a flying saucer would rescue the faithful.

A small circle gathered around her, known as the Seekers. Its most committed members included Charles Laughead, a physician at Michigan State College in East Lansing, and his wife Lillian; Laughead lost his post after the beliefs became public. Several believers quit jobs, gave away possessions and broke with skeptical relatives. In the days before the deadline the group waited more than once for promised pickups that never came, removing metal from their clothing on instruction from the messages.

On the night of 20 December they waited for a visitor at midnight. Nothing happened. After hours of silence and distress, at about 4:45 a.m. Martin received a new message: the little group, sitting all night long, had spread so much light that God had saved the world from destruction. Members who had avoided reporters began calling newspapers within hours and sought publicity in the days that followed. The group soon broke up under ridicule and police pressure, and Martin left Chicago. Under the name Sister Thedra she went on channeling messages from Sananda for decades, until her death in 1992.

concepts.title: The Study and Its Critics
concepts.contentHtml:
Leon Festinger, Henry Riecken and Stanley Schachter read about the prophecy in a newspaper and saw a test of ideas Festinger was developing. Their book When Prophecy Fails (1956) predicted that, under five conditions, believers faced with disconfirmation would cling harder and try to convert others: deep conviction; costly commitment that is hard to undo; a belief specific enough to be refuted; an undeniable refutation; and the support of fellow believers. The Oak Park members, who waited together, broadly fit the prediction; those in East Lansing, who waited mostly alone, tended to drift away. The book used pseudonyms throughout, so Martin appears as "Marian Keech".

The method was covert participant observation. The authors and hired observers joined without revealing their purpose, sometimes inventing psychic experiences to gain entry. At key moments observers made up a sizable share of the active members, believers took their arrival as a sign, and observers were at times pressed to lead meetings or offer messages. Critics argue that the researchers propped up the beliefs they were measuring and that their hypothesis shaped what they recorded. Deceiving people in crisis this way would not pass a modern ethics review.

Later tests were mixed. In 1962 Jane Hardyck and Marcia Braden reported on a small Christian group that spent weeks in fallout shelters awaiting nuclear attack; when none came, members kept their faith but did not step up recruiting. In a 2025 article in the Journal of the History of the Behavioral Sciences, Thomas Kelly drew on archival material to argue that the book's central claims are false, alleging fabricated messages and interference in a child welfare case; these allegations are recent and still debated.

concepts.title: The Watch Tower's Dates
concepts.contentHtml:
Date expectations also run through the history of the Jehovah's Witnesses, and they need careful statement. Charles Taze Russell (1852 to 1916), founder of the Bible Students, took from the former Millerite Nelson Barbour a chronology in which Christ's invisible presence had begun in 1874 and the "Gentile Times" of Luke 21:24 would end in 1914. Russell's writings presented 1914 as the year God's kingdom would be fully established in place of human governments. The outbreak of war that year seemed to followers a sign.

Under Russell's successor Joseph F. Rutherford, the campaign "Millions Now Living Will Never Die" (a 1918 talk, a 1920 booklet) pointed to 1925, when Abraham and other faithful men of old were expected to return to earthly life. A San Diego house, Beth Sarim, bought in 1929, was meant for them. Over time 1914 was reinterpreted as the year Christ was invisibly enthroned as king in heaven and the "last days" began, which remains Witness teaching.

The 1966 book Life Everlasting in Freedom of the Sons of God placed the end of 6,000 years of human history in autumn 1975, and publications suggested it would be fitting for Christ's thousand-year reign to begin then, while also warning against fixing a date. Membership grew fast before 1975 and stalled or dipped for a few years after. A 1980 Watchtower regretted statements that had made the hoped-for events seem "more of a probability than a mere possibility". In 1995 the teaching that the generation of 1914 would see the end was dropped. Witnesses describe such changes as growing light on Scripture and say no definite date was ever set; the sociologist Joseph Zygmunt (1970) traced a recurring cycle of expectation, disappointment and reinterpretation.

title: Modern Doomsday Dates
description: Harold Camping, the 2012 Maya misunderstanding, and why some groups survive a failed date

concepts.title: Harold Camping and 21 May 2011
concepts.contentHtml:
Harold Camping (1921 to 2013), a civil engineer turned Bible teacher, led Family Radio, a Christian broadcaster based in Oakland, California, with an international audience. He first predicted the end for September 1994, in a book titled 1994?, then blamed a miscalculation. His next date was built from numbers. He placed the Flood in 4990 BCE, read God's warning to Noah of "seven days" (Genesis 7:4) through the line in 2 Peter that one day is as a thousand years, and arrived at 7,000 years later: 2011. The Flood began on the seventeenth day of the second month, which he equated with 21 May. He added that from the crucifixion, which he dated to 1 April 33 CE, to 21 May 2011 was by his count 722,500 days, the square of 5 × 10 × 17, numbers he read as symbols of atonement, completeness and heaven.

The prediction: on 21 May 2011 the saved would be raptured, with a great earthquake rolling around the globe at 6 p.m. local time in each zone, followed by five months of judgment and the destruction of the world on 21 October. Family Radio and its supporters paid for thousands of billboards, and one retired New York transit worker reportedly spent about $140,000 on advertisements. Some followers quit jobs or spent their savings.

When 21 May passed, Camping said judgment had come spiritually and that the physical end would follow on 21 October. In June he had a stroke. October passed quietly. In March 2012 a letter from Camping acknowledged that he had been wrong and called his date-setting sinful. He died in 2013, and in 2018 Family Radio stopped airing his teaching.

concepts.title: 2012: A Calendar Misread
concepts.contentHtml:
The 2012 scare rested on a real calendar. The Classic Maya Long Count tallied days from a mythical starting point that corresponds, in the most widely used correlation, to 11 August 3114 BCE. Its large units included the b'ak'tun of 144,000 days, about 394 years. The starting point was written 13.0.0.0.0, and the count reached 13.0.0.0.0 again, the completion of thirteen b'ak'tuns, on 21 December 2012 (some scholars prefer 23 December). For the Maya, completing a great cycle was an occasion for ceremony.

Only one known ancient text discusses the 2012 date in any detail: Monument 6 from Tortuguero in Tabasco, Mexico, a seventh-century inscription, partly damaged, that mentions the completion of the thirteenth b'ak'tun and the god Bolon Yokte'. It describes no catastrophe. A stairway text found at La Corona, Guatemala, in 2012 also refers to the date, again without prophecy. Other inscriptions run far past it: one at Palenque projects a date in 4772 CE, and astronomical tables painted on a wall at Xultun, Guatemala, also announced in 2012, cover thousands of years.

The doomsday reading was modern. In the first edition of The Maya (1966) the archaeologist Michael Coe suggested that the Maya may have expected Armageddon at the end of the thirteenth b'ak'tun, a reading most Maya specialists later rejected. José Argüelles's The Mayan Factor (1987) and other New Age writers turned the date into a cosmic transformation, and others attached rogue planets ("Nibiru"), galactic alignments and solar storms. NASA scientists answered thousands of public questions, and Maya spokespeople in Guatemala rejected the doomsday reading, describing the date as the start of a new cycle.

concepts.title: How Groups Survive (and Some That Did Not)
concepts.contentHtml:
Research since Festinger suggests that disconfirmation rarely destroys a group by itself. In a 1985 article J. Gordon Melton argued that believers seldom experience a failed prophecy as a failure: they reinterpret it, often spiritually, and carry on because the group gives them community, worship and purpose beyond any single date. A review by Lorne Dawson (1999) and the collection Expecting Armageddon (2000), edited by Jon R. Stone, catalogue the usual moves. The event happened invisibly or spiritually (1914 for the Witnesses, 21 May for Camping). The arithmetic was off (Miller, Camping in 1994). The delay was a test that sifted true believers. Or the faithful themselves averted the disaster (the Seekers). Strong leadership, an organization with ongoing work and some distance from mocking outsiders all help.

Survival is not guaranteed. The Seekers dispersed within weeks. Chen Tao, a Taiwanese group led by Hon-Ming Chen that moved to Garland, Texas, announced that God would appear in bodily form at Chen's house on 31 March 1998. When nothing happened, Chen said he had misunderstood and offered to be stoned or crucified; no one accepted, and roughly two-thirds of members left. Camping's prediction left no organized movement behind. Millerism as a single movement dissolved, even though some of its fragments flourished.

The cases suggest a rough rule. Groups whose identity rests on one dated event, with little else holding them together, tend to fracture. Groups that have built institutions, rituals and relationships, and whose leaders can reframe the date, tend to absorb the blow, sometimes for centuries, as the Montanists did and as the Seventh-day Adventists and Jehovah's Witnesses still do. Münster was ended by siege.
